claims.text: Controlled oxygen or nitrogen interstitial doping is a method for overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off in high-entropy alloys.
Interstitial oxygen or nitrogen can generate ordered interstitial complexes in high-entropy alloys.
Ordered interstitial complexes impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Ordered interstitial complexes enhance strain hardening and ductility.
The base alloy has the composition Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi.
The undoped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloy has a severely distorted BCC structure.
Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi without oxygen or nitrogen addition can serve as the undoped baseline.
Oxygen- and nitrogen-containing variants of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi can be produced by arc melting, repeated remelting, and drop casting.
Arc melting, repeated remelting, and drop casting ensure a uniform distribution of interstitial atoms.
Subsequent heat treatments can promote interstitial ordering without causing undesired phase changes.
Ordered oxygen or nitrogen complexes form within the BCC lattice.
Interstitial complexes enhance both solid-solution strengthening and order strengthening.
The interstitially doped alloy will have higher yield strength than the undoped alloy.
The interstitially doped alloy will have greater ductility than the undoped alloy.
Oxygen- and nitrogen-doped Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloys can exhibit substantial yield strength and tensile elongation simultaneously.
The undoped baseline typically exhibits either high strength with low ductility or low strength with high ductility.
The effectiveness of interstitial doping is limited to concentration ranges in which ordered complexes form.
Extreme interstitial concentrations or different alloy systems may not produce the same strength-ductility balance.
Mechanical performance varies with whether oxygen or nitrogen is used as the interstitial element.
The strength and ductility improvements depend on interstitial concentration and processing parameters.
